body.p: This valuable study builds a novel auditory-motor paradigm to investigate how the brain learns associations between movements and their auditory consequences. Solid evidence is provided for early ERPs (50-100 ms latency) reflecting violations of established key-pitch mappings. The study is of potential interest to researchers studying audition, sensorimotor integration, or predictive coding, but some statistical analyses, however, could still be improved.
Summary:

Zhang et al. report on an ambitious study that investigates multiple aspects of the neural and behavioral underpinnings of auditory-motor surprisal in the context of an auditory-motor learning paradigm (piano keyboard). Using an intricate design comprising several sub-parts and control procedures, they report that early ERPs (50-100 ms latency) reflect violations of established key-pitch mappings.
Strengths:
The paradigm is quite intricate and at the same time addresses multiple aspects of auditory-motor learning and does so in an experimentally rigorous way.
Weaknesses:
In its current form, the analyses of the ERP data remain a weak point.
The following is the authors’ response to the original reviews.

disp-quote.p: Summary:

Zhang et al. report on an ambitious study that investigates multiple aspects of the neural and behavioral underpinnings of auditory-motor surprisal in the context of an auditory-motor learning paradigm (piano keyboard). Using an intricate design comprising several sub-parts and control procedures, they report that early ERPs (50-100 ms latency) reflect violations of established key-pitch mappings.
Strengths:
This is a carefully devised and executed study. The paradigm is quite intricate and, at the same time, addresses multiple aspects of auditory-motor learning, and does so in a rigorous way.
Weaknesses:

Perhaps because of the exhaustive approach, it is sometimes difficult to follow which parts of the experimental design the results come from; there are some questions regarding appropriate statistical methods, the inclusion/treatment of musical background in participants, and the nature (latency & extent) of the identified neural components that detect auditory-motor violations.
Summary:

Zhang et al. report an EEG study (n=18) of participants playing a keyboard where the correspondence between keys and pitches is varied to introduce sensory-motor mismatches (discrepancies between sensory inputs and expected sensory consequences of motor commands). They find that the auditory N100 amplitude is enhanced for the initial keystroke following a mapping switch but rapidly attenuates for subsequent keystrokes (showing rapid updating of the forward model), whereas the motor-related P50 amplitude only differentiates trained versus untrained mappings after 30 minutes of goal-directed practice (potentially showing timescales of inverse model updating). Using parallel univariate and mTRF decoding analyses, they conclude that forward models (mapping action to predicted sound) update almost instantly to track short-term context, while inverse models (mapping sound to motor commands) update slowly and require extended, targeted practice.
Strengths
(1) Methodological innovation:

The study utilizes an interesting, continuous auditory-motor paradigm that moves beyond standard trial-by-trial oddball designs, offering a more ecologically valid measure of trial-to-trial adaptation.
(2) Analytical elegance and rigor:

The combination of traditional univariate ERP analyses with multivariate temporal response function (mTRF) decoding is elegant, allowing the authors to successfully dissociate overlapping auditory and motor variance streams.
(3) The dissociation between the rapid adaptation of the N100 forward model and the slower adaptation of the P50 inverse model is interesting.
Weaknesses
(1) Confounded passive listening baseline:

The passive listening control condition lacks an orthogonal behavioural task (e.g., an occasional oddball detection task). Active playing inherently necessitates focused attention on auditory feedback to monitor performance, whereas passive playback does not. The globally weaker stimulus-evoked pattern at electrode Fz during passive listening strongly suggests that the absence of an N100 effect in this condition may simply reflect a lower state of attention, rather than isolating the absence of a motor-driven forward prediction, in particular because the pure sensory suprisal was also enhanced for "firsts" notes, so this could also lead to stronger N1, but this effect may be masked.

body.p: Here, our goal is to probe surprisal resulting from natural deviations of the expected sensorimotor map, and to test whether the observed response can be accounted for by the auditory components alone. In previous work, passive listening (without an explicit behavioral task) has been widely deemed sufficient to measure auditory surprisal (cf. Di Liberto 2020). Because the listener is not privy to the order of firsts and others within a session, any general attentional effects would be expected to influence all notes and therefore cannot explain the selective enhancement observed for “first” notes which follow a map change.

disp-quote.p: (2) Overclaimed theoretical novelty:

The conceptual framing leans excessively on the authors' specific "MirrorNet" framework, presenting foundational, decades-old tenets of the motor control literature (i.e., unsupervised exploration for forward models vs. supervised skill acquisition for inverse models; Wolpert, Jordan, both in the nineties) as their own novel "conjectures." This theory-heavy introduction obscures the paper's actual empirical contribution to the design and the interesting question regarding the distinct temporal adaptation scales of forward versus inverse models. I think some rewriting can improve the paper.

body.p: Thank you for pointing this out. It was not our intention to present the work of Wolpert etc. as a novel conjecture. We substantially revised the Introduction to emphasize that our contribution builds upon that theoretical framework and is also a study of how this framework evolves over time. We have cited Wolpert in the Introduction, and have now integrated the forward and inverse pathways more clearly into our hypotheses about the different effects of long- versus short-term sensorimotor experience on the MirrorNet framework.

disp-quote.p: (3) Misplaced surprisal terminology:

In a similar vein, I find the use of the term "auditory-motor surprisal" more theoretical grandstanding than actually useful. The significance statement claims to "extend this principle from sensory processing" but in fact, the concept of sensory motor unexpectedness is again a staple of the forward motor literature. Moreover, nowhere in the paper do they actually estimate sensorimotor surprisal. While the authors compute surprisal for their auditory baseline using IDyOM, their central sensorimotor analysis relies entirely on a simple categorical mismatch (first vs. subsequent keystrokes). The phenomenon can equally be referred to by its established nomenclature-"sensorimotor mismatch" or "sensory motor unexpectedness".

body.p: In the revised Introduction, we added a discussion of the relationship between surprisal and contextual predictions to clarify our terminology. In practice, the terms auditory-motor surprisal and sensorimotor mismatch refer to closely related phenomena. However, we chose the term surprisal because it emphasizes that prediction violations depend not only on the overall frequency of an event, but also on the context in which it occurs. In the surprisal literature, an event can be unexpected because it violates predictions generated from recent context, or long-term statistical regularities, or prior experience, even if the event itself is not objectively rare.

This distinction is important for our paradigm. A given note may occur frequently throughout the experiment and therefore is not rare in an absolute sense. Nevertheless, the same note may be highly surprising if it occurs immediately after a key-pitch map change, thus violating the participant's sensorimotor predictions. We therefore use the term surprisal to emphasize the role of contextual expectations rather than simple deviance or rarity.

We finally agree that, in the absence of an auditory-motor equivalent of models such as IDyOM, our study does not provide a continuous estimate of surprisal. Instead, we use the distinction between first and keystrokes as a categorical approximation of high- and low-surprisal events. Developing computational models that estimate continuous auditory-motor surprisal from the preceding sensorimotor context would be an interesting direction for future work, and we have added a note concerning this in the Conclusion.

disp-quote.p: (4) Incremental conceptual advance regarding the N100:

The paper frames the N100 finding as a major discovery, but as far as I know, the attenuation of the auditory N1 to self-generated sounds via accurate motor prediction-and its enhancement during sensorimotor mismatch - is one of the most heavily documented phenomena in the auditory-motor literature (e.g. Timm et al., 2013; Bendixen et al, 2012; 2013). As far as I'm concerned, the authors should clarify that the novelty lies in the novel, elegant design that provides a new way to correct for non-sensory-specific motor-induced attenuation, and characterizing the distinct adaptation timescales of forward versus inverse models -- not in demonstrating N100 modulation by sensorimotor mismatch, which is well-documented, AFAIC.

body.p: We agree now that the main finding of the paper is not discovering N100 as a signature of sensorimotor mismatch and we have revised the Introduction as discussed above. We now instead emphasize how it evolves over time and connect it to behavioural studies of sensorimotor perturbation where a behavioural adaptation is observed after one trial. We also incorporated the suggested literature on the N100 in the Introduction and Discussion because it shows that this neural signal has been previously seen in sensorimotor mismatch studies.

disp-quote.p: As very general feedback, I would encourage the authors to revise the manuscript so that it is much clearer which results come from which part of the experiment. For example, it took me a while to figure out that the ERP results in Figure 3 came solely from the 'Variable map playing' parts of the study (and perhaps only from the Pre-test phase?).

body.p: To improve clarity, we have rearranged the order of the figures and the respective text to organize the article into three main parts: the Variable Playing Task (Experiment I), the Training (Experiment II), and the TRF analysis (Experiment III). The paradigm panels are now closer to the Figure explaining their results. The Figure outlining how these tasks are carried out (previously Figure 2D) during one experimental session has been relegated to the supplementary materials.

disp-quote.p: Major:
(1) Statistics

(a) I couldn't shake the impression that the authors are treating the statistical analyses a bit too casually. Some analyses use parametric (ANOVA, t-test), others non-parametric tests (Wilcoxon) or bootstrapping, without explicitly reasoning for one or the other; there are also some examples where I believe no correction for multiple comparisons is applied, but should be applied (e.g., tests in Figure 4?).

body.p: We have added information in the Methods section to clarify the statistical choices. Here is a summary of our reasoning:

Bootstrapping (to find the difference between first and others): this was to account for the imbalance in class sizes and is more conservative than parametric alternatives. That being said, parametric tests do converge on the same result (Figure 6C, main effect of keystroke type in the 2-way within-subjects
ANOVA).

For Figure 4, we have replaced the pairwise tests with a more robust linear mixed-effects model to capture the relationship between the number of previous keystrokes and amplitude. This avoids multiple pairwise comparisons between conditions. However, the conclusions of the figure remain unchanged: the amplitude difference increases with the number of previous keystrokes.
Wilcoxon tests (subject-wise differences): With N = 18 participants, we do not meet the conventional threshold for normality (n > 30). The Wilcoxon test was therefore the appropriate choice.

Within-subjects ANOVA (training and first vs. others): A two-way within-subjects ANOVA was used when comparing two conditions. Within-subjects designs with N = 18 do not violate ANOVA assumptions in the same way between-subjects designs would, since the critical assumption is the sphericity of difference scores rather than marginal normality.

disp-quote.p: (b) Relatedly, I am not sure it is ok to run uncorrected statistical tests to identify 'time regions of interest', and to then zoom in on these and run additional statistical tests on them; this seems conspicuously like double dipping?

body.p: We did the uncorrected tests as an exploratory analysis, but we would have arrived at the same result if we chose timepoints of interest based on the literature (P50 and P100 were both well-documented; P250+ also potentially could have had an effect based on the literature (Lutz et al., 2013 for example), but in our experiment we did not find it).

disp-quote.p: (c) Comparing firsts versus other keystrokes: I wonder whether the bootstrapping procedure is necessary? In the MMN literature, this imbalance (oddball vs. standard) has not been an issue, as far as I am aware (or it has not been addressed?); I can follow the authors' reasoning for addressing this imbalance, but would feel more comfortable with the bootstrapping procedure if the authors can show that there is only a quantitative, but not a qualitative difference between statistics with bootstrapping vs. without bootstrapping (i.e. having a large imbalance between firsts and others keystrokes).

body.p: While bootstrapping is less commonly used in some ERP studies, we chose this approach because it provides a robust estimate under class imbalance between conditions, as is typical in oddball-like paradigms. The effect of firsts versus others keystrokes remains significant under standard parametric analyses, consistent with the main effect observed in the two-way ANOVA (Figure 6C).

disp-quote.p: (d) In addition, is it really correct to derive a null distribution only from the other keystrokes, as opposed to from both firsts and other keystrokes?

body.p: Our procedure defines a null distribution based on differences between randomly sampled other keystrokes. This allows us to quantify whether the observed amplitude difference between first and other keystrokes exceeds what would be expected from differences within the other condition alone. Under the null hypothesis, the first–other difference does not differ from the distribution of differences obtained by comparing randomly selected subsets of other keystrokes of equal size.

disp-quote.p: (2) Latency and duration of ERP differences

I was rather surprised by how early the effects appear to be. Coming back to the MMN paradigm: here, the latency of the peak MMN for oddballs is typically in the ~150-250 ms range, i.e. in P2 territory. Granted, the effect can be initiated in the N1 component range, but then it persists through P2; in the current paradigm, the effect is very selective to the N1 (or even the P50 latency for Pre- vs. Post-training comparisons, which puts this effect squarely in the primary auditory cortex). I would encourage the authors to explore this apparent discrepancy with respect to the MMN latency a bit more; is this related to passive vs. active paradigms? But why does the effect not persist and is seemingly restricted to a brief time window? Presumably, the auditory-motor mismatch, once it is detected, will have 'downstream' effects?

body.p: The early N100 effect has been reported multiple times in previous literature so we don't find this result surprising. It's possible that there are downstream effects that we're not seeing here. For example, we show in Figure S13 that the playing ERP is likely a linear sum of auditory and motor signals. The motor ERP also peaks at around 150, so in theory it could obscure the classic MMN. This point was mentioned in the Discussion (line 290).

disp-quote.p: (3) Musical background of participants

The authors state that some participants had more than 10 years of formal musical training, but that "none of the musically trained participants played piano as their primary instrument". How many of those nevertheless played piano? And how did this affect their performance? It would have been much cleaner to restrict participants to non-musicians...

I am not convinced that performance in the training task is an appropriate proxy for musicianship (as the authors suppose on page 10). In general, I think the consideration of musicianship in the study is by far the weakest and should probably be left out.

That being said, it is unfortunate that not more information on participants' background is provided, and that the authors did not exclude musicians, as this likely also has an impact on the results, since they presumably have had a stronger 'natural' key-pitch mapping than non-musicians.

body.p: Participants did fill out a questionnaire adapted from the Goldsmiths Musical Sophistication Index previously used in our laboratory’s other studies.We found no correlation with the GSI general score, nor the subscores. We have added the questionnaire results in the supplementary materials and the correlation plots for the overall musical sophistication score and the perceptual abilities score (the subscale most closely associated with the demands of our task). Nevertheless, for our use case, we do not believe that the questionnaire is more relevant for predicting sensorimotor learning abilities than the actual performance during training. For example, aspects of emotion and social engagement in music are also measured, which we don’t find to be relevant to musical learning abilities, and perceptual abilities are self-reported.

disp-quote.p: (4) How were peak amplitudes determined? (They should not be determined by simply picking the maximum, as this is susceptible to outliers, but instead as an average over a pre-defined time window.) In general, the description of methods would benefit from being more detailed.

body.p: We indeed computed the peak response as the maximum over a 40 ms window. However, given the large number of trials, and that the signal was already low-pass filtered to 30 Hz, corresponding to a ~33 ms cycle, it is unlikely that the estimate is significantly affected by transient noise or spurious peak fluctuations. The concern about outliers would be more relevant for single-trial data.

disp-quote.p: (5) Figure 3A and 6A 'Pre-training ERP' seem to be identical; why is that? Shouldn't Figure 3A essentially show the average of Figure 6A 'Pre-test ERP' and 6A 'Post-test ERP'?

body.p: Yes, it is indeed identical. Figure 3A is the variable map playing without the influence of any other tasks, therefore it’s the pre-training ERP.

disp-quote.p: (6) I had trouble following the results in Figure 4B/D. Why does 4B only go as far as 3 previous keystrokes, but 4D goes as far as 7? Maybe I am misunderstanding something here?

body.p: We showed only the contexts for which there were more than 300 trials, which we noted in the Methods section. There are fewer firsts in general, and fewer trials for higher numbers of keystrokes in the context. Therefore the 300 trial cutoff allows us to go up to 3 previous keystrokes for Figure 4B, but 7 previous keystrokes for Figure 4D.

disp-quote.p: (7) In Figures 3E and 3F, eyeballing and comparing the null and listen vs. null distributions (3E) with the First vs. Other distributions (3F), I had trouble wrapping my head around how the ones in 3F can be highly significantly different (p<0.001), while the others in 3E are not. (See also my question above re the calculation of the null distribution.)

body.p: Regarding Figure 3E, as detailed in the Methods section, the comparison between playing and listening was performed using a permutation test, whereas the p-values for comparisons between playing and null or listening and null were computed empirically as the proportion of values in the null distribution that exceeded the observed statistic. This is because playing and listening are both empirical (non-null) distributions, making a direct permutation test more appropriate for their comparison.

disp-quote.p: (8) Please clarify whether or not the decoders were compared to all keystrokes (firsts and others)?

body.p: The decoders were compared to all keystrokes in the main text (Figure 7), but a sized-match sample of firsts and others yielded the same conclusion (Figure S12).

disp-quote.p: (9) Last paragraph of Disentangling auditory...
If I understand it correctly, then neither ANOVA revealed an interaction; yet, the authors computed post-hoc pairwise comparisons nevertheless?

body.p: There is an interaction for P50 according to the ANOVA (Figure 6C). We followed up with post-hoc comparisons to investigate whether this interaction is driven by a particular key-pitch map.

disp-quote.p: (10) Figure S9: More information is needed re the TRF decoder; why such a short time window (as opposed to (showing) the ERP epoch -.2 to .5 s)? What does it mean for the decoder to have its peak at 0 s?

body.p: Since we used an inverse TRF formulation, the target reconstruction corresponds to a sparse impulse vector with value 1 at keystroke onsets and 0 elsewhere. As a result, only the temporal location at t=0 is of interest, with the expectation that the reconstruction should be flat outside this point. As a sanity check, we verified that averaging across onset-aligned windows reveals a clear peak at t=0, confirming that the model captures the expected temporal alignment between keystrokes and reconstructed responses.

disp-quote.p: Minor:
(1) Please include line numbers in the revised document to facilitate the review of the manuscript.
(2) Baseline period: either baseline correct to 100 ms, or show the entire 200 ms baseline period in the figures.

body.p: No baseline correction was applied to the ERP signals. Instead, data were re-referenced to the mastoids and band-pass filtered (1–30 Hz) to reduce slow drifts and high-frequency noise. As shown in Figure S5, the pre-stimulus baseline period does not exhibit systematic drift across conditions, consistent with stable baseline activity following preprocessing.

disp-quote.p: (3) I was surprised to read that the authors used Sennheiser 650 headphones - surely they introduce significant electrical interference?!

body.p: We have previously used headphones in EEG experiments in our lab without issues (cf. Cantisani 2023, Di Liberto 2020). In preprocessing, a notch filter at 50 Hz is applied to remove line noise, and ERP analyses are further low-pass filtered at 30 Hz to isolate the relevant evoked response components.

disp-quote.p: (4) ICA should be run on continuous data to avoid situations where an eyeblink cannot be accurately identified (and removed) because it's cut off by the epoch (and this way it would remain in the epoch and contribute noise).

body.p: ICA was indeed run on the continuous data (10 minutes for each task). We clarified this in the Methods section.

disp-quote.p: (5) The supplementary video was not available.

body.p: We have let the eLife team know about this.

disp-quote.p: (6) Figure 2F: I believe the x-axis tick marks should read Block1 and Block2, instead of Pre and Post? Please clarify (also in the corresponding text) whether this is averaged across Pre-training and Post-training sessions, or only for one of them?

body.p: Thank you for pointing out the error, it should indeed read block 1 and block 2, and has been updated. Both take place during the 30-minute training session, which consists of 2 blocks.

disp-quote.p: (7) Figure 3: It wasn't clear to me how only significant channels are shown.

body.p: We applied a mask so that only the significant channels are coloured according to amplitude difference. Non-significant channels are shown in white. The explanation for this is now found in Results > Experiment II > Effects of targeted skill acquisition training.

disp-quote.p: (8) For the decoder analyses, how did the authors determine that investigating/using the same electrodes for auditory vs. motor ERPs is appropriate? I am aware that ERPs evoked by the auditory cortex are maximal at fronto-central electrodes; is the same the case for motor ERPs?

body.p: We did not perform any pre-selection of channels for the decoder analyses. All channels were included in model training and prediction, allowing the decoder to learn data-driven spatial weights for reconstruction without imposing priors about channel relevance for auditory or motor processing.

disp-quote.p: (9) Figure 4A/C: The stems represent keystrokes during the Variable map Pre/Post test? This indicates that this particular participant often only played 3 notes?

body.p: Participants occasionally paused after producing short sequences of 3–5 notes. This behavior varied across individuals, with some producing near-continuous sequences with brief (< 1 s) pauses, and others inserting longer pauses (2–3 s) between melodic segments. Participants were instructed to generate short, varied melodic motifs and to avoid repeating identical sequences.

disp-quote.p: (10) Figure 5E: Were these based on size-matched comparisons, i.e. similar to the method the authors applied to the other analyses comparing first vs. other keystrokes?

body.p: The figure shows the means without size matching, but using size-matched comparisons doesn’t change the conclusions of the figures; we added this analysis in a supplementary figure.

disp-quote.p: (11) Figure 6C and 6G: there seem to only be 16 and 17 datapoints, respectively?

body.p: Figure 6C: We double-checked in the code and SVG file and there are indeed 18 subjects and 18 points.
Some points are not clearly visible in the figure due to very close overlapping.
Figure 6G: We unintentionally excluded one subject from the plot by setting the x-axis limit to between 2 and 4 on the training score. We have now adjusted the plot so that all subjects are visible.

disp-quote.p: (12) Figure 6C: Why an ROI here, but not elsewhere?

body.p: The ROI selection was based on prior ERP studies reporting robust auditory responses over central electrodes and motor-related error responses over frontal midline electrodes (Gehring 1993, Lutz 2013).
